cases.public_title: Faith Alone, but Not Faith Without Fruit
cases.short_label: Baptist sola fide and church discipline
cases.subtradition_scope: Southern Baptist + confessional/Reformed Baptist core; Free Will Baptist variation note
cases.app_availability: AVAILABLE — PAIRED RELEASE WITH ICC-002 (engineering gates)
cases.learner_question: If Baptists teach justification by faith alone, why can persistent sin or heresy result in church discipline or excommunication?
cases.key_distinction: Distinguish justification/standing before God from the congregation's judgment of visible profession, discipleship, and membership.
cases.resolution_summary: In Southern and confessional/Reformed Baptist theology, works do not merit justification. Repentance, sanctification, perseverance, and obedience are expected fruits/evidences of regeneration. Church discipline therefore addresses visible profession and ecclesial fellowship rather than functioning as a church cancellation of God's justification.
cases.internal_variation: Southern and confessional/Reformed Baptists typically resolve the tension through perseverance and evidentiary fruit. Free Will Baptists likewise deny salvation by works but allow that a genuinely saved person may later make shipwreck of faith and be lost.
cases.interfaith_significance: The case shows why 'faith alone' is not equivalent to 'conduct does not matter.' It reveals substantial shared Christian concern for repentance, holiness, perseverance, accountability, and discipleship while preserving real differences in the theology of justification and security.
cases.does_not_prove: It does not make Baptist and Latter-day Saint soteriology identical; it does not claim all Baptists share one perseverance model; and it does not treat excommunication as a direct determination of God's hidden judgment of regeneration.
cases.learner_cue_copy: How can faith alone and church discipline both fit Baptist theology? See the distinction.

cases.public_title: By Grace, After All We Can Do
cases.short_label: Latter-day Saint grace and "after all we can do"
cases.subtradition_scope: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (canonical scripture + official General Conference and Gospel Topics teaching)
cases.app_availability: AVAILABLE — PAIRED RELEASE WITH ICC-001 (engineering gates)
cases.learner_question: If Latter-day Saints believe they are saved by grace, why does the Book of Mormon say "after all we can do," and why do the Articles of Faith say salvation comes "by obedience to the laws and ordinances of the Gospel"? Does that mean Latter-day Saints earn salvation by works?
cases.key_distinction: Distinguish the source of salvation (the grace of Jesus Christ alone, which no one can earn) from the response salvation calls for (repentance, faith, obedience, and enduring), and distinguish "saved" in the broad sense (resurrection and redemption offered to all) from exaltation (the fulness of eternal life received through covenant).
cases.resolution_summary: In Latter-day Saint teaching, no one earns salvation. The Book of Mormon states that it is "only in and through the grace of God" that anyone is saved (2 Nephi 10:24), and official teaching states plainly that "we cannot earn our way into heaven" and that salvation "cannot be bought with the currency of obedience" (Dieter F. Uchtdorf, "The Gift of Grace," April 2015 General Conference). "After all we can do" (2 Nephi 25:23) does not mean grace is paid out once human effort is exhausted; in the Book of Mormon's own usage "all we could do" is repentance (Alma 24:11). Obedience to the laws and ordinances of the gospel (Articles of Faith 1:3) is the covenant response through which a person receives and keeps receiving the gift, not a price paid for it. Official teaching describes obedience as "the reaching out of our mortal hand to receive this sacred gift" and grace as "the divine help or strength extended to us through the Atonement" (Gospel Topics: Grace) that enables the disciple to be "perfect in Christ" (Moroni 10:32).
cases.internal_variation: Latter-day Saints have read "after" in 2 Nephi 25:23 two ways: as a temporal sequence (grace completes what effort begins) and, in the reading emphasized by recent official teaching, as "in spite of" or "regardless of" all we can do. Both readings deny that salvation is earned; they differ on how to describe the relationship between effort and gift. The doctrine also uses a graded vocabulary: universal salvation from physical death through resurrection, redemption from sin through faith and repentance, and exaltation through covenant obedience. A Latter-day Saint who says "saved" may mean any of these, which is where interfaith conversations most often talk past each other.
cases.interfaith_significance: The case shows why "after all we can do" is not equivalent to "Latter-day Saints earn salvation by works." It reveals substantial shared Christian ground: salvation is a gift of grace through Jesus Christ that no one can merit, and true faith is expected to bear fruit in repentance and obedience. It preserves the real difference, which is not grace versus works but the covenantal structure through which grace is received and the distinction between salvation and exaltation. Read beside ICC-001, it shows both traditions carrying the same fault line in mirror image: a Baptist slogan that sounds like conduct is irrelevant, and a Latter-day Saint slogan that sounds like grace is a reward.
cases.does_not_prove: It does not make Latter-day Saint and Baptist or Reformed soteriology identical; it does not resolve the differences over imputed versus infused righteousness, ordinances as conditions of covenant, or the doctrine of exaltation; and it does not claim that every Latter-day Saint has always articulated grace without a works-emphasis. It settles what the sources teach, not how every member has spoken.
cases.learner_cue_copy: How can Latter-day Saints say they are saved by grace "after all we can do"? See the distinction.
